title: Roadmap 1: language core (OOP, equality, collections, generics)
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: OOP design, the equals/hashCode contract, how HashMap and Python dict/deque behave internally, and generics versus type hints in Java and Python.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: In Java, which capability does an abstract class have that an interface does not?

options.text: Declaring non-static instance fields that hold per-object mutable state.
options.why: Right: interfaces may only declare constants (implicitly public static final), so per-instance state needs a class.

options.text: Declaring method signatures with no body so subclasses must implement them.
options.why: Interfaces declare abstract methods too, so this does not separate the two.

options.text: Providing default method implementations that subclasses inherit as-is.
options.why: Interfaces have had default methods since Java 8, so this is not unique.

options.text: Being implemented by several unrelated classes spread across different hierarchies.
options.why: That is the strength of interfaces; a class can extend only one abstract class.

questions.explanation: Use an interface for a capability contract that unrelated classes can adopt; use an abstract class when subclasses share state and partial implementation. Prefer composition when you only want to reuse code, since a class can extend just one parent.

questions.prompt: In Java, if a.equals(b) returns true, then a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode().

options.text: True
options.why: Right: this is the core of the equals/hashCode contract that hash-based collections rely on.

options.text: False
options.why: The contract requires equal objects to have equal hash codes; only the reverse (equal hashes imply equal objects) is not required.

questions.explanation: The reverse is not required: unequal objects may share a hash code (a collision). Overriding equals without hashCode breaks HashMap and HashSet lookups.

options.text: Both return null, and the entry stays in the map but is effectively unreachable.
options.why: Right: k now hashes to a different bucket, and a fresh Key(1) finds the old bucket but fails equals against the mutated key.

options.text: get(k) returns "x" because the same object reference is passed again.
options.why: HashMap hashes the key first; the changed hash points at a different bucket, so identity alone does not help.

options.text: get(new Key(1)) returns "x" because the stored hash was cached and matches.
options.why: The cached hash matches, but equals then compares id 1 with the mutated id 2 and fails.

options.text: Both throw ConcurrentModificationException because the key changed.
options.why: That exception is for structural modification during iteration, not for mutated keys.

questions.explanation: Mutating a field used in equals/hashCode after insertion orphans the entry: a silent leak and lookup bug. Use immutable keys (String, records, frozen dataclasses).

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Which statements about java.util.HashMap in OpenJDK 8 and later are true?

options.text: With the default load factor 0.75, the table doubles once the entry count exceeds 0.75 times capacity.
options.why: Right: default capacity 16 resizes at 12 entries to 32 buckets.

options.text: A bucket with 8 or more colliding entries can be converted to a red-black tree.
options.why: Right: treeification needs the table to be at least 64 buckets; smaller tables resize instead.

options.text: It allows one null key and any number of null values.
options.why: Right: the null key hashes to bucket 0; Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap reject nulls.

options.text: Iteration returns entries in insertion order.
options.why: That is LinkedHashMap; HashMap order depends on hashes and bucket layout.

options.text: Concurrent put calls from several threads are safe without extra locking.
options.why: HashMap is not thread-safe; use ConcurrentHashMap or external synchronization.

questions.explanation: Know the numbers: 16 initial buckets, 0.75 load factor, treeify at 8 per bucket (with at least 64 buckets). Lookups degrade from O(1) average toward O(log n) in a treeified bin rather than O(n).

questions.prompt: A Python BFS over a large graph uses queue = [start] and queue.pop(0) in its loop, and it is slow. What is the best fix?

options.text: Use collections.deque and popleft(), which removes from the front in O(1).
options.why: Right: deque is a doubly linked list of blocks with O(1) appends and pops at both ends.

options.text: Keep the list but call queue.reverse() once so that pop() takes from the end instead.
options.why: Reversing once does not help new items, which are appended at the other end each iteration.

options.text: Switch the queue to a set so membership checks become O(1).
options.why: A set has no order, so it cannot act as a FIFO queue.

options.text: Switch to heapq so the smallest node is always popped first.
options.why: A heap gives priority order at O(log n), not FIFO, and changes the traversal.

questions.explanation: list.pop(0) shifts every remaining element, so it costs O(n) per pop and O(n^2) overall. Java parallels: ArrayDeque beats LinkedList as a queue and a stack.

questions.prompt: A Python function needs any object that has a read() method, without forcing classes to inherit from a base class, and mypy should check it. Which construct fits?

options.text: typing.Protocol, which uses structural subtyping on the method shape.
options.why: Right: any class with a compatible read() satisfies the protocol with no inheritance.

options.text: abc.ABC with @abstractmethod, which every implementing class must subclass.
options.why: ABC is nominal typing: classes must inherit (or register) to be accepted.

options.text: @dataclass, which generates the read() method from declared fields.
options.why: Dataclasses generate __init__, __repr__ and __eq__, not behaviour like read().

options.text: A TypeVar bound to object, which constrains the argument to have read().
options.why: A bound of object accepts anything and says nothing about read().

questions.explanation: Protocol is the Python analogue of Go-style interfaces: duck typing that a type checker can verify. Use ABC when you want an enforced inheritance hierarchy or shared template methods.

questions.prompt: In Python 3, a class that defines __eq__ but not __hash__ is still hashable and uses the default identity-based hash.

options.text: True
options.why: Python sets __hash__ to None when __eq__ is defined without __hash__, so instances become unhashable.

options.text: False
options.why: Right: defining __eq__ alone sets __hash__ to None, so putting instances in a set or dict key raises TypeError.

questions.explanation: Define both, or use @dataclass(frozen=True), which generates __eq__ and __hash__ together from the fields. A plain @dataclass with eq=True and no frozen also sets __hash__ to None.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Which statements about Java generics are true?

options.text: A List<? extends Number> can be read as Number but you cannot add non-null elements to it.
options.why: Right: the compiler cannot know which subtype the list holds (producer extends).

options.text: A List<? super Integer> accepts add(Integer) but reads back only as Object.
options.why: Right: consumer super; the actual element type could be any supertype of Integer.

options.text: Type arguments are erased at runtime, so new T() and x instanceof List<String> do not compile.
options.why: Right: erasure removes T and String; only the raw type remains in bytecode.

options.text: List<Integer> is a subtype of List<Number> because Integer extends Number.
options.why: Generics are invariant; allowing it would let you add a Double to a list of Integer.

options.text: A primitive such as int can be used directly as a type argument, as in List<int>.
options.why: Type arguments must be reference types; use List<Integer> and accept boxing.

questions.explanation: Remember PECS: producer extends, consumer super. Python offers a different model: TypeVar and Generic are checked only by mypy or pyright and have no runtime effect.
